speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I sat and listened to my hon. friend, I hope with courtesy and without a single interruption although he spoke for twenty minutes, and I think he should accord to me the courtesy of allowing me to have at least one completed sentence without in interjection. My hon. friend is getting along in years but he still shows the impetuosity of youth. He does not seem to be able to contain himself for more than half a minute. It is a nice spring morning and if he would just contain himself in peace and relax a little I am sure he would find it very good for the nervous system.
The smile of my hon. friend is just as welcome as the spring morning.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not know why my hon. friend from Shelburne-Yarmouth refers to the question of the tariff in association with the United States of America because if there is one country in the world which has been noted for its high tariff it has been that country, and if there is one country in the world which formulates its tariff policy to suit the needs of its own people without regard to the rest of the world it is the United States. I do not complain of that because that is their right and their privilege. But my hon. friend must not attempt to make it appear that we must place ourselves in the position where we are to defer entirely to the whims and whimsies of out friends to the south. My hon. friend must realize, and I think the people of the United States themselves would be the first to say, that the question of our tariff is entirely a matter for ourselves, and they would be the last to take exception to our altering the tariff on any item as in our judgment we deemed to be in our own best interests.
My hon. friend from Shelburne-Yarmouth has taken the position that the excise tax of three per cent ought to be imposed on fish imported into this country from Newfoundland. If my hon. friends from Antigonish-Guysborough and Queens-Lunenburg were here I am sure they would unanimously take exception to any such proposal. The question of our relationship with Newfoundland, as my hon. friend knows, is a very old story. It goes back over a long period of years, and
it has been distinctly understood that we would never impose any form of taxation against the importation of fish from Newfoundland, which after all is the only commodity they have to sell to us, and there is the further fact that the balance of trade between Canada and Newfoundland has for all time been very largely in our favour. But the fishing industry itself in Nova Scotia is vitally interested in the importation, duty free, of fish from Newfoundland, for a very considerable portion of the fishing industry of Nova Scotia is based upon the processing of Newfoundland fish for re-export.
At one o'clock the committee took recess.
The committee resumed at three o'clock.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when the committee rose at one o'clock I was dealing with the question of the imposition of a duty or tax upon importations of fish from Newfoundland. I had pointed out that the subject was by no means new. It has been discussed over a number of decades, and I do not know of any branch of the fishing industry that has been more opposed in the past and so far as I am aware, is still opposed to such a tax or duty than those associated with the ownership, operation and management of the Lunenburg fleet. Apart from the consideration that the importation of salt fish from Newfoundland has hitherto proven a profitable branch of the Canadian fishing industry, there was the further consideration that one of the strongest arguments used by those who were opposed to the imposition of the duty or tax was that if by any chance we impeded the importation of their fish we would invite reprisals on the part of Newfoundland, perhaps quite properly so, and that those reprisals would take the form, amongst others, of not permitting the sale of bait to our bankers. If they were not able to get their bait in Newfoundland ports it would mean their return periodically to the ports of the maritime provinces, with consequent loss of time and also loss of profit in their fishing operations. So that while I do not for one moment suggest that when these considerations are borne in mind the last word has been said, I do submit that they are of such moment as to preclude, for the time being at least, our entertaining the imposition of such a duty. As I do not wish to take up the time of the committee further in passing the estimates of my colleague the Acting Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Duranleau), I will content myself with these few observations.

Mr. Chairman, about the last thing I would wish to do at this late stage of the proceedings would be to hold up the estimates of the minister, but by reason of the fact that certain statements were made Tuesday evening and again to-day of a derogatory character as to the quality of the salt produced in the riding I have the honour to represent, I feel I am drawn into this controversy, and that something in the interests of truth, justice and accuracy should be said with respect to this product. The Malagash salt industry was established in Malagash some years ago, and in normal times it employs upwards of a hundred hands. It was felt at the time of its establishment that it would more or less interlock with the fishing industry of Nova Scotia. The district in which the industry has been developed is not by any means what might be termed affluent; the people there have been struggling along under most severe handicaps particularly during the last couple of years. To show the community spirit on the part of the employers as well as the employees, the committee will be interested to learn that a cooperative working arrangement has been entered into by them.
Now, the derogatory statements made by the hon. members for Antigonish-Guysborough and Shelburne-Yarmouth with respect to the quality of this salt in the curing of fish ought, I think, to be answered by those in the industry who know what they are talking about. In this connection I am going to read into the record certain telegrams I have received from those who know the fish business with respect to the value of this salt in the curing of fish. The first is from S. R. Giifin and Son, of Goldboro, Nova Scotia:
Malagash' salt best we ever used for hard cured dried codfish,-never dampen again after being dried or turn red in hot countries if held any time as sometimes happens when fish are cured with salt such as Turks island.
The next telegram is from Austin E. Nickerson carrying on business in the constituency of the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston):	He says:
Understand discussion regarding Malagash salt now going on. Wish to advise that we have used Malagash salt solely for the past ten years with absolutely good results, and on account of good keeping qualities of our fish have been able to obtain extra prices. Have never seen any indication of red fish, but there is a slight sediment, apparently gravel, in salt, but that can be overcome by proper methods of curing. Have used many other salts, including German, and prefer Malagash.

Another telegram is from McCormack and Zatzman, Limited, of St. John, New Brunswick. They say:
Regarding Malagash fishery salt, we have used thousands of tons of it in the last few years, shipping a large portion of our products to southern countries, with absolutely no spoilage losses and without cold storage charges, whereas when formerly using solar or sea salt we have experienced losses in these markets. Malagash is the best salt we know of for all cures of smoked herring and Gaspereau, and you will be making no mistake whatever in doing everything possible to increase the use of Malagash salt by Canadian fishermen.
Another telegram is from A. Haydon, Magdalen islands. It is dated from New Glasgow and is as follows:
Visiting here to-day noticed controversy in house on salt and cures of fish. After an experience of many years supervising fish packing in Nova Scotia and Magdalen islands, wish to state I have used Malagash mined salt on the curing of codfish and mackerel, and have found it very satisfactory. My opinion is that codfish cured with mined salt has a much milder flavour than fish cured with solar salt.
That point was emphasized this morning by the hon. Minister of Finance. I have another telegram which comes from the fisheries experimental station at Halifax. This station, I understand, is under the biological board, which is composed of representatives of the fish industry, the fisheries department and the universities. The telegram reads as follows:
Regarding Malagash salt, can state that if proper precautions are taken mined salts will prevent red fish. Tests here recent lots of Malagash salt, there was very little sediment on fish, and we have proof that large amount of equal salt has been mined at Malagash.
The last telegram I desire to read is from the Malagash Salt Company, Limited. They say:
If Hansard records statement that Malagash salt leaves red streaks on the fish and that sediment is unsatisfactory . . . correction should be made. Many people make such statements without advising themselves on recent result with Malagash salt. Their conclusions are really based on results that are out of date.
Such erroneous statements on Malagash salt have been very damaging and have retarded the development of the industry the importance of which you fully appreciate. Malagash is cheapest of few salts available here that does not produce red fish. The fishermen's losses from reddening is now recognized by Halifax station officials and trade generally as a terrific handicap. Malagash being germ free is definitely stated on page twelve of Harrison's honorary research council paper number eleven. Regarding sediment Dr. Leim, director Halifax station advises this difficulty no longer a factor with salt from vein that we have worked past two years also on reddening. Our sales talks on fishery salt all based on American bureau fishery

findings and recommendations bulletins numbers 884 and 919 and Malagash salts are those most nearly meeting the specifications recommended. If such evidence is acceptable it shows the fishermen's troubles are in a large measure due to failure to adopt the scientific information available to them. The Cockfield-Brown report draws that conclusion. S. R. Giffin and Son, Goldboro, claim our salt best for hard dry cure. A. E. Nickerson, Yarmouth, claims they did not have a loss from reddening on shipment many million pounds cut fish to American market where colour is also an all important factor. McCormack and Zatzman, St. John, very large users have had greatest satisfaction our salt. W. H. Smith, Lunenburg Sea Products, Lunenburg, reports Malagash salt very satisfactory for their processed fish trade. W. C. Smith and Company, Lunenburg, have also long appreciated tile better keeping qualities Malagash salt. Fisheries department Gaspe cure demonstrator Peter Mercier wrote us last fall Malagash salt only salt with which he could produce that cure on the Magdalen Islands. While fish cured by these firms represent practically all different cures produced in maritimes rve have very many maritime references including Robichaud, member of McLean commission. Several Newfoundland as well Morue Francaise St. Pierre among our best and largest customers and highly satisfied _ with results over several years on their cure similar to Lunenburg. In many of these cures the difference in return from the use of salt of the specification recommended will more than pay for all the salt used and Canadian Malagash salt meets the requirements.
I have every sympathy, as every hon. member from Nova Scotia has, for the fishing industry; we all realize that it has suffered a great deal and that, due to world conditions, it is in a most unfavourable position to-day. But I cannot see why a blow should be struck at another legitimate Canadian industry, the Malagash salt industry, by depreciating the quality of their product, which I think has been conclusively demonstrated by the telegrams I have just read to be equal to any other salt produced for the curing of fish. I think in fairness to this industry the hon. gentlemen opposite who have spoken in this way should withdraw or qualify their statements, as they seem to be labouring under a misapprehension. Of course, if hon. gentlemen opposite are not interested in industry in the maritime provinces they will not withdraw, but I contend that this is a legitimate industry which should not be dealt a blow on the floor of this house with respect to the quality of its products, which a great many fishermen say is eminently suitable for the purposes for which they use it.
One other point and I am through. When this industry was started a seam was developed which contained some material which caused reddening. That vein or seam has been abandoned, and to-day they are developing another seam producing an excellent quality
of salt for fisheries purposes. In addition, with the scientific improvements that have been adopted by this company, they are able to produce a salt that is claimed by many fishermen to be better than any other salt used in the curing of fish.

I listened with a great deal of interest to the discussion that took place last evening and this forenoon in connection with the fishing industry. I have been interested in that industry for the past thirty years, and I was especially interested in the remarks of my hon. friend from Shelburne-Yarmouth, who seems to be the champion of the fishing industry in western Nova Scotia.
I cannot agree with many of the suggestions made by the hon. gentleman last night and this morning, but on one point I do agree with him. That is that the government was badly advised in that they did not grant the full two weeks extension of the season to May 31, though they did give us five days more than we really expected at first. Of course, when the six weeks season was granted last winter it was understood that two weeks would be taken off the other end of the season, which would close on May 15 instead of May 31. Those six weeks were of great benefit to the fishermen of western Nova Scotia, and it is a fact that they made that bargain. Of course they expected then that they would secure their usual catch of lobsters during the month of March and April, but unfortunately March this year was a very severe month along the coast of Nova Scotia, during which few if any lobsters were taken. I have the figures here showing the catch during the months of March and April for the past three years. They are:

I made representations to the government asking that the fishermen be given the extra two weeks in order to make up for the loss they sustained particularly during March, but in their judgment the government did not see fit to grant that extension. I think they made a mistake, but I am not going to censure them for that. I believe the fishermen in western Nova Scotia are grateful for the extra five days, which will compensate them somewhat.
With regard to the drain on the lobsters, or the conservation of the fisheries, that is an
Supply-Fisheries

exploded idea; there are just as many lobsters in the sea to-day as ever there were. As I say, I have been connected with the industry for some thirty years or more, and in each of those thirty years we were told that unless something was done in connection with the lobster season they soon would be extinct. What has been the result? Last year the catch was better than it had been for many years, and I noticed in the press the other day that when the season opened in Cape Breton they had the largest catch they have ever had. I believe in conservation, but I also believe that the department should be advised by those who know something about the industry. I am not censuring the government for what they have done; perhaps they were wise, but I think they go too much on theory rather than on practice.
I was particularly interested in the remarks of my hon. friend for Shelburne-Yarmouth. He had nothing to offer but complaints and criticisms. He criticized this government for everything that has been done by the Department of Fisheries since this government came into power, but I want to tell the committee that in the two years it has been in power this government has done more for the fishermen than the government of my hon. friend did in the nine years they were in power. They never turned a hand to do anything for the fishermen. During the few months that the present Minister of Finance was in charge of the Fisheries department, he did more for the fishing industry of Canada than any minister who has ever had charge of that department, and it was with extreme regret that the industry learned that he was giving u,p that portfolio to take the more responsible one of Finance. Had the Minister of Finance retained the portfolio of Fisheries, I believe he would have done something worth while for the fishing industry, for which nothing has ever been done by any minister who has ever managed the department.
My hon. friend speaks about the excise duty and the sales tax on salt. In my opinion our Canadian salt industry should receive the support of the fishing industry. It is good salt. I have had experience in the use of Malagash salt, for we have used quantities of it, and while, as the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough said the other night, it does leave a little scum on top of the pickle after it is made, that does not interfere with the curing of the fish. We have used thousands of tons of it and have found it very good salt indeed. We have used, occasionally, Mediterranean salt, and sometimes Turk's island salt, because vessels comfMr. Short.]
ing up from the West Indies can bring Turk's island salt to Nova Scotia cheaper than we can obtain the Malagash salt delivered to our plants. But so far as quality is concerned, the Malagash salt is perfectly good. It is a reliable brand and if it is properly used there is no reason why the fishermen of Nova Scotia should not be using Nova Scotia salt instead of Mediterranean or West Indies salt.
My hon. friend from Shelburne-Yarmouth spoke about a bounty on fish. That started, of course, with the Lunenburg fleet; they asked for a bounty. I suggest that if the government grants a bounty on salt fish it will have to give a bounty on fresh and smoked fish. Moreover, it will have to extend the bounty to farm produce, lumber and all other industries. I think it would be a mistake to begin giving a bounty to this or that industry. We are not in a position to grant bounties to all the natural industries of the country, and in my opinion the government would be ill-advised to give a bounty to any one particular class of fish produced in Canada.
As regards the sales tax on packages and coverings, this, of course, will include the tins as well as the outside package for canned fish. It includes the parchment covers for fillets, haddies and kippers, as well as the package. But this sales tax, it must be remembered, applies to every other industry as well as fish; it applies to every business. If we protest on behalf of the fishing industry, we must protest also on behalf of fruit and poultry, the butter and milk industry and every other. It is absolutely necessary for us to raise taxes this year from every source possible, and if it is unavoidable to tax the packages used for fish, then I say that the fishing industry will accept the tax just as other industries are accepting it. If, however, exemptions are to be made, the fishing industry must get the benefit of them along with the others. Personally, I have heard no complaints from those engaged in the fishing industry. Many of these people interested in the industry are carrying on a very large business in Nova Scotia, and I have had no complaints from them with regard to packages. They intimate, that they realize the necessity for raising taxes from every possible source. The fishing industry will have to bear its share along with the others, but if exemptions are made then, as I say, we feel that we must be included.
The fishing industry has been hard hit, particularly in the last two years. During that time there is not a concern engaged in Ihe industry that has broken even. But

Supply-Fisheries
they are not discouraged. We feel that we are over the worst of it now, and I believe that conditions are going to improve. When they do, the fishing industry, along with others, will benefit.
I do not intend to say anything further, because I realize that the committee is anxious to get through, but I must say that this government is doing what it can for the industry, and I believe it is disposed to do all in its power to further the interests of the fishermen. My hon. friend from Shel-burne-Yarmouth spoke of the report submitted by Cockfield, Brown & Company. He called it a dud, saying that there was nothing in it. I say that there is a great deal in it. If many of the suggestions contained in that report are carried out, as I believe they will be carried out by this government eventually, the result will be highly beneficial to the industry, and I think that the Minister of Finance, the former Minister of Fisheries, deserves a great deal of credit from the industry for having employed this firm, and for the report that has been submitted.
Has the minister received any official request for cooperation on behalf of the Quebec provincial government with regard to the maritime fisheries in the gulf and the St. Lawrence river?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: Not to my knowledge.

Of course, the minister's
answer does not satisfy me to any great extent. I understand him to say that he has no knowledge of any communication. I should like to know precisely whether the Department of Fisheries of the province of Quebec has sent a letter or a telegram or any other communication asking for the cooperation of the federal government, with a view to improving the situation in the maritime fisheries, especially in the last six months.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
I am informed by
my officials that during the past two years no communication has been received from the department of fisheries of the province of Quebec.

I am very much surprised to hear that. As was stated on the floor of the house during the discussion which took place some weeks ago on the motion of the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay (Mr. Casgrain), a great number of people from the Gaspe coast, especially from the counties of Gaspe and Bonaventure came to Quebec to interview the government and ask that necessary representations be made by the
Quebec government to secure the cooperation of the federal government. I hold in my hand a copy of the memorandum submitted by that delegation to the provincial government, and I should like to quote as follows:
We affirm our confidence in the diplomacy of the provincial cabinet to conduct negotiations in view of joining with the Ottawa government and to regularize our position by way of cooperation. Since a few years, under the influence of new knowledge and the requirements of commerce, a quiet revolution has taken place in the domain of fisheries that we cannot ignore. Consequently many new initiatives are now on the order of the day; a ministry of fisheries has even been created to look after this evolution.
That memorandum was submitted to the provincial government on March 19, 1932. Since that time the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay has moved very eloquently a resolution which was agreed to unanimously. This resolution asked this government to cooperate with the provincial government of Quebec in order to give assistance to the maritime fisheries. I understand that such a policy of cooperation cannot be carried on or attempted by the federal government alone. It is not an easy thing for this government to intervene. But I have no hesitation to say that this question of the development of fisheries is as vital to the province of Quebec as it is to the maritime provinces and British Columbia. In discussing this question I should like to refer to a memorandum prepared by one of the fisheries' experts in the province of Quebec, dealing with the development of fisheries in that province.
During the period from 1900 to 1920, thanks to modern scientific discoveries, numerous scientists have applied themselves intensely and successfully to the study of the sea. They have succeeded in making many discoveries relating to fish migration and have formulated many laws which have resulted in increasing the productivity of the fisheries. These studies, still practically at their inception, are being prosecuted actively year by year. In Europe alone, fourteen nations, by common consent have divided the waters in which scientific research is to be carried on. They have grouped themselves into a great intellectual cooperative society. Universities are popularizing the practical knowledge to be derived from their investigations in connection with fishing. The complete courses are already fairly extensive and cover from three to five years.
It is now generally admitted that if accurate knowledge of the different soils is essential to rational farming, some knowledge
Supply-Fisheries

of the sea is equally essential to the profitable pursuit of fishing. In his book entitled The Products of the Sea Dr. Loir writes:
Just as rational farming proceeds from chemical laboratories, so rational fishing finds in oceanographical laboratories all the elements essential to its development.
The natural resources conservation commission, which .has devoted several of its sittings to the study of the fishery problem, has given expression to similar views. If we are to believe the high authorities who have given the deepest thought to this serious question, scientific institutions, study circles, research and demonstration centres have become as indispensable to the promotion of the fishing industry and its proper administration as they are in the case of agriculture. The solution of the problem lies in study and teaching: a technical staff is necessary to provide the required guidance. It would take too long to enumerate the different subjects one must master to qualify as an expert or specialist in fishery matters.
Scientists have not only confined themselves to the thorough investigation of marine life but they have devoted themselves no less intensely to the transformation of the industrial processes in vogue during the last century and to the improvement of commercial methods with a view to obtaining a better return. By 1900 these men were associated together under the name of International Sea Exploration Committee, which is now divided into the following three great intellectual associations:
The International Sea Exploration Committee.
The International Mediterranean Committee.
The International Fishery Research Committee of North America.
The United States, France and Canada are members of the latter committee.
As the fisheries of the province of Quebec have been entirely under the control of the provincial government since 1922 and as the fishery map of our province, according to the annual report on fisheries issued by Ottawa, seems to have been deleted from that of the dominion, it goes without saying that we are not represented on this International Fishery Research Committee of North America. We do not belong to any group as we do in the case of agriculture, and the official circles of our province have appeared to be perfectly satisfied with this state of affairs, at least up to the last session of the legislature. They have not even thought of providing us with an intelligent nomenclature of the fish varieties to be found in the province of Quebec. Our provincial fishery service is composed of

a staff which lacks scientific, industrial and commercial training. After eight years of groping there are no institutions of learning, there are no demonstration establishments and the service is .powerless and absolutely incapable of solving the many problems which arise. The lamentable failure of its undertakings in connection with porpoise destruction, refrigeration construction and so on justifies amply the criticism which has been directed against it. Establishments of this kind have existed for several years in all parts of Europe, even in the least advanced countries such as Esthonia, Bulgaria and so on. Establishments are to be found in the British, Italian and French colonies and even Indo-China. The fishermen of the province of Quebec are placed at a disadvantage when compared with those of Indo-Ohina who enjoy a leadership which keeps in contact with modem progress.
For about twenty-five years prior to 1922 public opinion in the province of Quebec was misled by the constantly reiterated claim that the organization of our fisheries depended upon the question of jurisdiction. This formed the subject of endless discussions between Quebec and Ottawa. It will be remembered that since 1898 there has been a constant conflict between the governments at Quebec and Ottawa with regard to jurisdiction. Three cases have been submitted by the courts of the province of Quebec for decision by the privy council. British Columbia had to cope with the same difficulty but that province was parotical enough to use them as a pretext to delay the organization of its fisheries. In spite of its conflicts, it never ceased to cooperate with Ottawa, and at the present time that province possesses two marine biological stations located at Prince Rupert and Nanaimo, and also a well organized and complete fishery service which, according to the statement of the former Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) on April 3, 1922, costs the federal treasury $400,000 a year and yields but a trifling revenue. On the other hand, the maritime provinces led by practical men have applied themselves with sincerity and perseverance to the study of the various aspects of the fishing industry. Instead of fighting the federal authorities and confusing the minds of the people, they have cooperated with them in order to strengthen their hand. As early as 1900 the maritime provinces had a marine biological station located at St. Andrews, the first of its kind in Canada. Later, about 1922, under the direction of Professor Cobb, of Washington university, they founded the Halifax Fishery School at a cost of $100,000 provided by the federal government. A few

Supply-Fisheries
years later, a second biological station, more up to date and better equipped, was constructed at Halifax, again at the expense of the federal government. All these institutions contribute to the training of industrial executives and others who fill the most difficult positions in the fisheries service.
Towards 1915 there was organized the Canadian Fisheries Association, to which the best minds of the country, representatives of the federal and provincial governments, of the universities and of big business, contribute their valuable cooperation, and, at the annual meetings, which mark epochs in the life of the movement, discuss all questions affecting the fishing industry. It is this well organized and effective influence, which the province of Quebec has always ignored, that, on July 12, 1928, brought about the appointment of a deputy minister of fisheries separate from the Department of Marine, and, in 1930, the creation of a department of fisheries.
It is likewise to the efforts and recommendations of this association that we owe the reform that has been going on for fifteen years of the whole federal service; information offices in all the provinces except Quebec, a service composed of trained and disciplined men, marine biological laboratories at St. Andrews, Halifax, Prince Rupert and Nanaimo, improved transportation by rail and water of the products of the sea, and all the advantages that have brought about the development of the fisheries of the other provinces to the point where they command the attention even of foreigners.

I understood from his words that he wished me to continue reading the letter I sent last year to the Minister of Fisheries. The rest of that letter reads:
With reference to the protection of our waters, I wish to draw your attention in particular to the fact that there exists at present in the gulf and in the northern part of the gulf, a nuisance which causes incalculable damage to our fishers and which will become a menace in the future: porpoises. It has been calculated that their number' reaches approximately 100,000 and that they consume 1,000,000 tons of small fish every year. These statistics are astounding. It permits us to doubt the utility and usefulness of fishing regulations as long as the porpoises continue to thrive in our waters in such considerable numbers. They take away more merchantable fish in a week tnan could be taken away by any illegal fishing in many seasons.
In the past the poirpoise schools limited their activities to the entrance of the Saguenay or thereabouts. We are therefore convinced that this section was the home of a very intense maritime life for it was sufficient during many centuries to furnish them the quantity of food necessary for life. No biological research has as yet been conducted in this section, but simple observation permits us to state that it is the point on which converged during centuries many species of fish coming from the Atlantic and from the sources of the St, Lawrence. When this fact is more clearly demonstrated, we must assuredly be convinced that the destruction of porpoises interests the maritime provinces and the province of Ontario as well as Quebec, and that therefore the problem is a national one, and consequently a federal one.
From the fact that the porpoises for the last ten years stay less in the district of the Saguenay than for centuries previous, we must conclude that they no longer find sufficient nourishment, and that the river St. Lawrence is so impoverished by their depredations that they are forced to emigrate towards the gulf.
Their destructive work is continually increasing and prevents all profitable fishing operations. It is now common knowledge that many species of fish, which it is claimed go up the river to spawn, have considerably diminished in the last 25 or 50 years.
The government of Quebec undertook to solve this problem but did not succeed; it has, however, become too serious to be abandoned. We can but conclude that the federal parliament alone must see to the removal of a danger which threatens the whole of Canada. When it was a question of lessening the harmful effect of dogfish and seals, etc., affecting the fishing industry of certain provinces, the federal government deemed it proper to intervene; it cannot ignore the problem caused by the presence of porpoises in our waters. Since it concerns the future of the St. Lawrence, the problem is serious enough to warrant the attention of the federal government, on whose part action or cooperation is essential.
In concluding I submit that the federal government, even though the agreement of 1922 be not revised and remain as it is at present, must, in Quebec as well as elsewhere, join in finding a solution for all our fishing problems, and that we also have all possible reasons to claim the organization by it of a modern, competent fishing service, well furnished, and which the provincial government cannot render complete for different reasons.
There exist, I am perfectly convinced, many gaps in our fishing administration, a field of great enterprise where the influence of your department could be beneficently employed and which demands its intervention. To arrive at a practical result I can suggest nothing better, in the first place, than the establishment of a local fisheries bureau in order to establish a contact with our population. This bureau would be the starting point for many other useful enterprises which would develop in due course.
I attach a great importance to the question which I have tried to lay before you, and dare to hope that you will give this problem your prompt and serious attention. I do not doubt that all the members of the province of Quebec will give it their enthusiastic approval.
Hoping to have the occasion of discussing this matter with the expert of your department,
I beg you to accept, dear Mr. Rhodes, my kindest regards,
0. Gagnon.

I can only repeat now to the minister, who loves his province so well and who knows the condition of the fisheries there, the demand I made to his predecessor, and ask him to try his best to remedy the detrimental situation which was brought about by the transfer of maritime fisheries to the government of Quebec in 1922.

As the hon. member for Bonaventure said a moment ago, in the province of Quebec there is an abnormal situation. The federal government has transferred the whole of the maritime fisheries of the St. Lawrence river to the provincial government; nevertheless, it kept under its supervision and control that part of the maritime fisheries pertaining to the Magdalen islands, which, as you know, belong to the province of Quebec. We find, therefore, on the one hand, that the maritime fisheries of the province of Quebec in the St. Lawrence river have been transferred to the government of that province, while on the other hand, the maritime fisheries in the gulf of St. Lawrence have been transferred to Halifax, because the fisheries of the Magdalen islands in the gulf of St. Lawrence are under the control of Nova Scotia.
It appears, therefore, that this agreement, which was entered into, is not only illegal and ultra vires but is absolutely ridiculous, and it is detrimental to the interests of the fishermen. I appreciate the fact that the minister cannot immediately put an end to that agreement, because it is bilateral: both the federal and the provincial governments are committed to it, so that without first having received a request from the provincial government for its abrogation, the minister cannot put an end to it. I have in my hand documents showing that the provincial government does not at present wish to have the agreement abrogated, but if that is not possible just now, owing to the fact that the government of the province of Quebec does not wish it, nevertheless I think we ought to do something for the fisheries of that province. And one thing which in my opinion is absolutely necessary is the establishment of a fisheries office in Quebec, which would begin to supervise conditions in the province, make a thorough investigation and suggest to the government the proper steps to be taken to meet the situation that exists there.
A moment ago my hon. friend from Comox-Alberni showed some surprise at the figures I gave. I have here the figures showing the revenue of the fishermen of Canada for the year 1930, and I find that the per capita revenue in British Columbia was $1,194.
Who says that?
I am giving this from the statistics for 1930.
But who says it?

As my hon. friend knows,
the Year Book is published by the Department of Trade and Commerce, but the articles are not signed. But these figures have been compiled by the technicians and experts of that department. They were taken from the memorandum submitted to the provincial government by the fishermen of Bonaventure and Gaspe. I did not invent these figures myself; they were quoted in the memorandum submitted by the fishermen who asked the provincial government to do something to put an end to the illegal agreement which was entered into in 1922. As I say, the per capita revenue of fishermen in British Columbia for the year 1930 was SI,194, whereas in the province of Quebec it was only $206. According to the officials of the department, during the last ten years the annual average revenue of the fishermen of Quebec has diminished rather than grown. In 1920, the average earnings were $398, while by 1930, they had dropped to $206.
I do not wish to take up the time of the committee any longer except to say that I respond to the invitation given by the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil) who stated that I ought to ask the government to help the fishermen and farmers of Quebec. I do not intend to ask hon. members to read my speeches, but on April IS last I was courageous enough to ask the government of the day to do for the eastern farmer as much as it was doing for the western farmer.
Before taking my seat, I ask the minister to try to satisfy the fishermen of Quebec and establish a fishery bureau which I know will prove to be as useful as similar establishments which have been created in connection with other departments, especially the, Department of Agriculture. On April 15 last I stated that dual establishment, dual legislation and dual administration in connection with the same subjects were not in the interests of the people. It is absolutely against the public interests for the government of Quebec and the federal government to devote their energies concurrently to the same subjects, but we cannot change the situation brought about by confederation. This situation can be remedied only by calling together as soon as possible a provincial conference to study ways and means of preventing dual

administration. Until this conference takes place or until other steps are taken to remedy the situation, I think we ought to do for fisheries what we have done for agriculture and other industries.
While it is true the federal government has transferred the administration of fisheries to the province of Quebec, it should still take an interest in the fishermen. Notwithstanding the sympathy the provincial government may have for the fishermen, notwithstanding its desire to help fishermen in general, it is unable to solve the problem. The problem of the fisheries is not only provincial in character, it is national and even international. Every year fishermen come from Newfoundland to fish along the coast of Charlevoix-Saguenay and Gaspe. The provincial authorities are unable to put a stop to this practice; the provincial government has no authority to take any steps to remedy the situation. In 1922 the federal government had a boat equipped for this service, which boat was managed by experts. The gentleman at the head of that particular branch of the department in Quebec was Doctor Bernier, who has a wide knowledge of all questions affecting the fisheries. This gentleman has been in the department for almost ten years and has rendered great service to the fishermen.
I think I have spoken long enough, and I thank the hon. Minister of Fisheries for listening patiently to my remarks. Should he receive a letter from the provincial government, I ask the minister to rise above party prejudices and recognize that this is not only a provincial problem but rather one that is national in scope. I ask him to forget party differences and to do his best to help the provincial authorities in this regard.
